selected_passages.title: SBF, riding high on FTX, reportedly offered $5B to Trump to cancel President re-run
selected_passages.text: Come Tuesday, our eyes will be trained on the Manhattan Federal Court for the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried, the disgraced cryptocurrency entrepreneur accused of orchestrating “one of the biggest financial frauds in American history”: the multibillion-dollar collapse of FTX, the crypto exchange he founded and led. SBF, as he’s known, has pleaded not-guilty to some seven charges of fraud and conspiracy. But, as we wait to hear both his version and the government’s version of what happened, there will be another tale recounting how things played out: “Going Infinite,” a book by Michael Lewis chronicling the rise and fall of SBF, is set to debut on the first day of the trial. The episode has fired up a lot of people, indignant at what they feel was too-easy treatment for someone who many believe brought down the whole crypto house. 60 Minutes got rightly community noted here. How is it that SBF is _still_ getting super positive media coverage when the media has nothing good to say about the founders that have actually created things and brought value into the world? https://t.co/VPV1ORVHqf — tobi lutke (@tobi) October 2, 2023 The germination of “Going Infinite” sounds as unlikely as the story

selected_passages.text: A new class action lawsuit filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case, filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, argues that Google “siphons off” news publishers’ content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means. It also specifically cites new AI technologies like Google’s Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem. In the complaint, Helena World Chronicle, which owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas, argues that Google is “starving the free press” by sharing publishers’ content on Google, losing them “billions of dollars.” In addition to new AI technologies, the suit points to Google’s older question-and-answer technologies, like the “Knowledge Graph” launched in May 2012, as part of the problem. “When a user searches for information on a topic, Google displays a ‘Knowledge Panel’ to the right of the search results. selected_passages.title: 5 things we learned so far about the Google antitrust case
selected_passages.text: Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified Monday in the U.S. government’s antitrust trial against the company. The executive defended Google’s business tactics, including its deal with Apple and other partners to make Google the default search engine. The lawsuit stems from a 2020 antitrust claim over Google’s dominance in the online search market. The claim is separate from one filed in January by the Department of Justice, along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, that aims to “halt Google’s anticompetitive scheme, unwind Google’s monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising.” The government has argued that Google uses its platforms and deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, thus hindering competitors from accessing the data they’d need to improve their products. Google argues that it’s just doing business. Everybody wants Google as the default engine because it’s the best. That doesn’t make its actions illegal, the company says. Monday’s trial hearing revealed plenty of juicy tidbits, including the $26.3 billion Google spent making itself the default search engine across platforms in 2021, how Google tried to take it further and have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones and more. Google paid $26

selected_passages.title: Is Google Search better than the rest? And is that fair?
selected_passages.text: Google’s results? This month, Wired posted an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray, which alleged that Google had accidentally revealed during the trial that it manipulates people’s search queries for maximum ad revenue. The example given was replacing a search for “children’s clothing” with “NIKOLAI-brand kidswear”. Loading Google rejected this in very strong terms, saying the piece was misleading and inaccurate while denying ever altering search terms. Wired removed the article for not meeting its standards, but the degree to which it was shared on social media and boosted in write-ups at other outlets shows just how willing people are to accept foul play on Google’s part. selected_passages.text: A new class action lawsuit filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case, filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, argues that Google “siphons off” news publishers’ content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means. It also specifically cites new AI technologies like Google’s Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem. In the complaint, Helena World Chronicle, which owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas, argues that Google is “starving the free press” by sharing publishers’ content on Google, losing them “billions of dollars.” In addition to new AI technologies, the suit points to Google’s older question-and-answer technologies, like the “Knowledge Graph” launched in May 2012, as part of the problem. “When a user searches for information on a topic, Google displays a ‘Knowledge Panel’ to the right of the search results. Google argues that it’s just doing business. Everybody wants Google as the default engine because it’s the best. That doesn’t make its actions illegal, the company says. Monday’s trial hearing revealed plenty of juicy tidbits, including the $26.3 billion Google spent making itself the default search engine across platforms in 2021, how Google tried to take it further and have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones and more. Google paid $26

selected_passages.text: A new class action lawsuit filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case, filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, argues that Google “siphons off” news publishers’ content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means. It also specifically cites new AI technologies like Google’s Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem. In the complaint, Helena World Chronicle, which owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas, argues that Google is “starving the free press” by sharing publishers’ content on Google, losing them “billions of dollars.” In addition to new AI technologies, the suit points to Google’s older question-and-answer technologies, like the “Knowledge Graph” launched in May 2012, as part of the problem. “When a user searches for information on a topic, Google displays a ‘Knowledge Panel’ to the right of the search results. selected_passages.title: 5 things we learned so far about the Google antitrust case
selected_passages.text: Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified Monday in the U.S. government’s antitrust trial against the company. The executive defended Google’s business tactics, including its deal with Apple and other partners to make Google the default search engine. The lawsuit stems from a 2020 antitrust claim over Google’s dominance in the online search market. The claim is separate from one filed in January by the Department of Justice, along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, that aims to “halt Google’s anticompetitive scheme, unwind Google’s monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising.” The government has argued that Google uses its platforms and deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, thus hindering competitors from accessing the data they’d need to improve their products. Google argues that it’s just doing business. Everybody wants Google as the default engine because it’s the best. That doesn’t make its actions illegal, the company says. Monday’s trial hearing revealed plenty of juicy tidbits, including the $26.3 billion Google spent making itself the default search engine across platforms in 2021, how Google tried to take it further and have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones and more. Google paid $26

Loading Google rejected this in very strong terms, saying the piece was misleading and inaccurate while denying ever altering search terms. Wired removed the article for not meeting its standards, but the degree to which it was shared on social media and boosted in write-ups at other outlets shows just how willing people are to accept foul play on Google’s part. A suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling follows the company at all times. Grey herself is a former vice-president at DuckDuckGo, a privacy-focused company founded explicitly to counter giants such as Google. selected_passages.title: 5 things we learned so far about the Google antitrust case
selected_passages.text: Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified Monday in the U.S. government’s antitrust trial against the company. The executive defended Google’s business tactics, including its deal with Apple and other partners to make Google the default search engine. The lawsuit stems from a 2020 antitrust claim over Google’s dominance in the online search market. The claim is separate from one filed in January by the Department of Justice, along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, that aims to “halt Google’s anticompetitive scheme, unwind Google’s monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising.” The government has argued that Google uses its platforms and deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, thus hindering competitors from accessing the data they’d need to improve their products. Google argues that it’s just doing business. Everybody wants Google as the default engine because it’s the best. That doesn’t make its actions illegal, the company says. Monday’s trial hearing revealed plenty of juicy tidbits, including the $26.3 billion Google spent making itself the default search engine across platforms in 2021, how Google tried to take it further and have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones and more. Google paid $26

selected_passages.text: A new class action lawsuit filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case, filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, argues that Google “siphons off” news publishers’ content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means. It also specifically cites new AI technologies like Google’s Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem. In the complaint, Helena World Chronicle, which owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas, argues that Google is “starving the free press” by sharing publishers’ content on Google, losing them “billions of dollars.” In addition to new AI technologies, the suit points to Google’s older question-and-answer technologies, like the “Knowledge Graph” launched in May 2012, as part of the problem. “When a user searches for information on a topic, Google displays a ‘Knowledge Panel’ to the right of the search results. selected_passages.text: Come Tuesday, our eyes will be trained on the Manhattan Federal Court for the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried, the disgraced cryptocurrency entrepreneur accused of orchestrating “one of the biggest financial frauds in American history”: the multibillion-dollar collapse of FTX, the crypto exchange he founded and led. SBF, as he’s known, has pleaded not-guilty to some seven charges of fraud and conspiracy. But, as we wait to hear both his version and the government’s version of what happened, there will be another tale recounting how things played out: “Going Infinite,” a book by Michael Lewis chronicling the rise and fall of SBF, is set to debut on the first day of the trial. The episode has fired up a lot of people, indignant at what they feel was too-easy treatment for someone who many believe brought down the whole crypto house. 60 Minutes got rightly community noted here. selected_passages.title: 5 things we learned so far about the Google antitrust case
selected_passages.text: Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified Monday in the U.S. government’s antitrust trial against the company. The executive defended Google’s business tactics, including its deal with Apple and other partners to make Google the default search engine. The lawsuit stems from a 2020 antitrust claim over Google’s dominance in the online search market. The claim is separate from one filed in January by the Department of Justice, along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, that aims to “halt Google’s anticompetitive scheme, unwind Google’s monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising.” The government has argued that Google uses its platforms and deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, thus hindering competitors from accessing the data they’d need to improve their products. Google argues that it’s just doing business. Everybody wants Google as the default engine because it’s the best. That doesn’t make its actions illegal, the company says. Monday’s trial hearing revealed plenty of juicy tidbits, including the $26.3 billion Google spent making itself the default search engine across platforms in 2021, how Google tried to take it further and have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones and more. selected_passages.title: Is Sam Bankman-Fried a bad ‘man’ or a good ‘boy’? Lawyers swap opening statements before first witnesses take the stand
selected_passages.text: Who is Sam Bankman-Fried, the former CEO of crypto exchange FTX? Is he a liar and a fraud? Or did he act in good faith, and like many a startup founder, fly too close to the sun? And as one former federal prosecutor put it: “The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point.” The 31-year-old co-founded FTX in 2019; within a few years the once third-largest crypto exchange’s valuation hit $32 billion at its peak. It’s now trying to claw back any funds to distribute to creditors. But how did the once third-largest crypto exchange get here? Before FTX, Bankman-Fried co-founded crypto-trading firm Alameda Research in 2017. He co-founded FTX in 2019 as a complement to Alameda, to help bring in revenue and liquidity for the trading arm. Within two years, more than 80 investors provided about $2 billion in capital to FTX, helping Bankman-Fried propel his vision into a reality. In January 2022, the company raised $400 million in a Series C round, boosting its valuation to $32 billion. That was its last round of public funding. selected_passages.title: 5 things we learned so far about the Google antitrust case
selected_passages.text: Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified Monday in the U.S. government’s antitrust trial against the company. The executive defended Google’s business tactics, including its deal with Apple and other partners to make Google the default search engine. The lawsuit stems from a 2020 antitrust claim over Google’s dominance in the online search market. The claim is separate from one filed in January by the Department of Justice, along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, that aims to “halt Google’s anticompetitive scheme, unwind Google’s monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising.” The government has argued that Google uses its platforms and deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, thus hindering competitors from accessing the data they’d need to improve their products. Google argues that it’s just doing business. Everybody wants Google as the default engine because it’s the best. That doesn’t make its actions illegal, the company says. Monday’s trial hearing revealed plenty of juicy tidbits, including the $26.3 billion Google spent making itself the default search engine across platforms in 2021, how Google tried to take it further and have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones and more. selected_passages.title: News publisher files class action antitrust suit against Google, citing AI’s harms to their bottom line
selected_passages.text: A new class action lawsuit filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case, filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, argues that Google “siphons off” news publishers’ content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means. It also specifically cites new AI technologies like Google’s Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem. selected_passages.text: Google’s results? This month, Wired posted an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray, which alleged that Google had accidentally revealed during the trial that it manipulates people’s search queries for maximum ad revenue. The example given was replacing a search for “children’s clothing” with “NIKOLAI-brand kidswear”. Loading Google rejected this in very strong terms, saying the piece was misleading and inaccurate while denying ever altering search terms. Wired removed the article for not meeting its standards, but the degree to which it was shared on social media and boosted in write-ups at other outlets shows just how willing people are to accept foul play on Google’s part. A suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling follows the company at all times. Grey herself is a former vice-president at DuckDuckGo, a privacy-focused company founded explicitly to counter giants such as Google. She admits that she may have misinterpreted the evidence, but maintains that Google manipulates Search to maximise ad revenue. So what does Google say? selected_passages.title: News publisher files class action antitrust suit against Google, citing AI’s harms to their bottom line
selected_passages.text: A new class action lawsuit filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case, filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, argues that Google “siphons off” news publishers’ content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means. It also specifically cites new AI technologies like Google’s Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem. In the complaint, Helena World Chronicle, which owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas, argues that Google is “starving the free press” by sharing publishers’ content on Google, losing them “billions of dollars.” In addition to new AI technologies, the suit points to Google’s older question-and-answer technologies, like the “Knowledge Graph” launched in May 2012, as part of the problem. “When a user searches for information on a topic, Google displays a ‘Knowledge Panel’ to the right of the search results. - Google's internal chat logs were deleted despite being subject to a litigation hold.

Helena World Chronicle, LLC has filed a class action antitrust lawsuit against Google and Alphabet in the U.S. District Court in D.C., alleging that Google's AI technologies, including Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard, along with older features like the Knowledge Graph, are siphoning content, readers, and ad revenue from news publishers. The suit claims these practices violate the Sherman Act and Clayton Act by discouraging users from visiting publisher websites, potentially causing publishers to lose 20-40% of their traffic, and seeks an injunction requiring consent for using publisher data to train AI models.

[raw:sources/News_publisher_files_class_action_antitrust_suit_against_Google_citing_AI_s_harms_to_their_bottom_line]
A new class action lawsuit filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case, filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, argues that Google “siphons off” news publishers’ content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means. It also specifically cites new AI technologies like Google’s Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

selected_passages.text: For the US, which has to prove that Google somehow broke the law to achieve the status quo, this legal case could be an uphill battle. But for the rest of us, it offers a rare opportunity for some insight into what the tech giant does with its enormous market share. Is it still focused on being the best? Or, as has been alleged, does it use its ubiquity to squeeze us for money even at the expense of product quality? How ‘organic’ are Google’s results? This month, Wired posted an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray, which alleged that Google had accidentally revealed during the trial that it manipulates people’s search queries for maximum ad revenue. The example given was replacing a search for “children’s clothing” with “NIKOLAI-brand kidswear”. Loading Google rejected this in very strong terms, saying the piece was misleading and inaccurate while denying ever altering search terms. Wired removed the article for not meeting its standards, but the degree to which it was shared on social media and boosted in write-ups at other outlets shows just how willing people are to accept foul play on Google’s part. A suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling follows the company at all times.

selected_passages.text: Grey herself is a former vice-president at DuckDuckGo, a privacy-focused company founded explicitly to counter giants such as Google. She admits that she may have misinterpreted the evidence, but maintains that Google manipulates Search to maximise ad revenue. So what does Google say? selected_passages.title: raw:sources/Is_Google_Search_better_than_the_rest_And_is_that_fair
selected_passages.text: For the US, which has to prove that Google somehow broke the law to achieve the status quo, this legal case could be an uphill battle. But for the rest of us, it offers a rare opportunity for some insight into what the tech giant does with its enormous market share. Is it still focused on being the best? Or, as has been alleged, does it use its ubiquity to squeeze us for money even at the expense of product quality? How ‘organic’ are Google’s results? This month, Wired posted an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray, which alleged that Google had accidentally revealed during the trial that it manipulates people’s search queries for maximum ad revenue. The example given was replacing a search for “children’s clothing” with “NIKOLAI-brand kidswear”. Loading Google rejected this in very strong terms, saying the piece was misleading and inaccurate while denying ever altering search terms. Wired removed the article for not meeting its standards, but the degree to which it was shared on social media and boosted in write-ups at other outlets shows just how willing people are to accept foul play on Google’s part. A suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling follows the company at all times.

selected_passages.title: raw:sources/Is_Google_Search_better_than_the_rest_And_is_that_fair
selected_passages.text: Grey herself is a former vice-president at DuckDuckGo, a privacy-focused company founded explicitly to counter giants such as Google. She admits that she may have misinterpreted the evidence, but maintains that Google manipulates Search to maximise ad revenue. So what does Google say? In a post on X, Google’s official search liaison, Danny Sullivan, said ad systems do not affect the organic results, i.e. the list of blue links in search results that are not sponsored. “Ad keyword matching is a long-standing and well-known process that is designed to connect people to relevant ads. A separate process, which has nothing to do with ads, is used to match organic results to a query,” he said. “It’s no secret that Google Search looks beyond the specific words in a query to better understand their meaning ... If you make a spelling mistake, or search for a term that’s not on a page but where the page has a close synonym, or if you aren’t even sure exactly how to search for something, our meaning matching systems help.” It is true that some search queries result in more ads than others, and what ads you get can vary wildly depending on your request, which is the result of the keyword matching Google uses to sell ads. But Google denies pushing users towards the most monetisable subjects.

selected_passages.title: sources/5_things_we_learned_so_far_about_the_Google_antitrust_case
selected_passages.text:
- Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to make itself the default search engine.
- Approximately $18 billion of the payment went directly to Apple.
- Google's deal with Apple has been in place since 2003.
- When users switch their browser homepage to Google, they perform 15% more searches.
- When users switch away from Google, their searches drop by 27%.
- Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella offered to spend $15 billion annually to make Bing the default on Apple devices.
- Google gets 16 times more data than Bing every day.
- The DOJ accused Google of systematically destroying chat messages via the history-off option.
- Pichai changed the history-off default for chat in February to comply with a litigation hold.
- The trial is expected to continue for several weeks.
- The case is compared to the 1990s U.S. trial against Microsoft.
- If ruled against Google, the outcome could resemble the Microsoft settlement.
- Google might be required to turn over collected data to other search engines.
- The FTC sued Amazon in September for anticompetitive strategies.
- The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over its third-party app policies.
- There is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook regarding Instagram and WhatsApp.
- Google's legal chief David Drummond sent an angry letter to Microsoft in 2005.
- The letter accused Microsoft's Internet Explorer default setting as anticompetitive.
- Google's internal chat logs were deleted despite being subject to a litigation hold.
- Pichai testified on October 28 regarding the search head's revelations.
- The DOJ filed a separate claim in January alongside eight states.

This month, Wired posted an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray, which alleged that Google had accidentally revealed during the trial that it manipulates people’s search queries for maximum ad revenue. [raw:sources/Is_Google_Search_better_than_the_rest_And_is_that_fair]

She admits that she may have misinterpreted the evidence, but maintains that Google manipulates Search to maximise ad revenue. So what does Google say? A separate process, which has nothing to do with ads, is used to match organic results to a query,” he said. “It’s no secret that Google Search looks beyond the specific words in a query to better understand their meaning ... If you make a spelling mistake, or search for a term that’s not on a page but where the page has a close synonym, or if you aren’t even sure exactly how to search for something, our meaning matching systems help.” It is true that some search queries result in more ads than others, and what ads you get can vary wildly depending on your request, which is the result of the keyword matching Google uses to sell ads. But Google denies pushing users towards the most monetisable subjects.

Or, as has been alleged, does it use its ubiquity to squeeze us for money even at the expense of product quality? How ‘organic’ are Google’s results? The example given was replacing a search for “children’s clothing” with “NIKOLAI-brand kidswear”. Loading Google rejected this in very strong terms, saying the piece was misleading and inaccurate while denying ever altering search terms. Wired removed the article for not meeting its standards, but the degree to which it was shared on social media and boosted in write-ups at other outlets shows just how willing people are to accept foul play on Google’s part. A separate process, which has nothing to do with ads, is used to match organic results to a query,” he said. “It’s no secret that Google Search looks beyond the specific words in a query to better understand their meaning ... If you make a spelling mistake, or search for a term that’s not on a page but where the page has a close synonym, or if you aren’t even sure exactly how to search for something, our meaning matching systems help.” It is true that some search queries result in more ads than others, and what ads you get can vary wildly depending on your request, which is the result of the keyword matching Google uses to sell ads. Helena World Chronicle, LLC has filed a class action antitrust lawsuit against Google and Alphabet in the U.S. District Court in D.C., alleging that Google's AI technologies, including Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard, along with older features like the Knowledge Graph, are siphoning content, readers, and ad revenue from news publishers. The suit claims these practices violate the Sherman Act and Clayton Act by discouraging users from visiting publisher websites, potentially causing publishers to lose 20-40% of their traffic, and seeks an injunction requiring consent for using publisher data to train AI models.

selected_passages.title: sources/5_things_we_learned_so_far_about_the_Google_antitrust_case
selected_passages.text:
- Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to make itself the default search engine.
- Approximately $18 billion of the payment went directly to Apple.
- Google's deal with Apple has been in place since 2003.
- When users switch their browser homepage to Google, they perform 15% more searches.
- When users switch away from Google, their searches drop by 27%.
- Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella offered to spend $15 billion annually to make Bing the default on Apple devices.
- Google gets 16 times more data than Bing every day.
- The DOJ accused Google of systematically destroying chat messages via the history-off option.
- Pichai changed the history-off default for chat in February to comply with a litigation hold.
- The trial is expected to continue for several weeks.
- The case is compared to the 1990s U.S. trial against Microsoft.
- If ruled against Google, the outcome could resemble the Microsoft settlement.
- Google might be required to turn over collected data to other search engines.
- The FTC sued Amazon in September for anticompetitive strategies.
- The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over its third-party app policies.
- There is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook regarding Instagram and WhatsApp.
- Google's legal chief David Drummond sent an angry letter to Microsoft in 2005.
- The letter accused Microsoft's Internet Explorer default setting as anticompetitive.
- Google's internal chat logs were deleted despite being subject to a litigation hold.
- Pichai testified on October 28 regarding the search head's revelations.
- The DOJ filed a separate claim in January alongside eight states.

context:
[sources/Apple_defends_Google_Search_deal_in_court_There_wasn_t_a_valid_alternative]
- Eddy Cue testified that there was no valid alternative to Google Search for Apple devices at the time of the deal.
- The Information Services Agreement (ISA) makes Google the default search engine on Apple products in exchange for billions in payments.
- Apple believes in protecting user privacy but also maintains a strong partnership with Google, creating a central tension in the trial.
- Cue argued that showing users alternative search engines during setup would degrade the user experience and slow down device onboarding.
- The Justice Department questions whether Apple's choice of Google is based on product quality or financial incentives.

[sources/5_things_we_learned_so_far_about_the_Google_antitrust_case]
Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified in a U.S. antitrust trial defending the company's $26.3 billion spending to secure default search engine status across platforms, including a major deal with Apple. The Department of Justice argues these tactics block competition and hinder rivals from accessing necessary data, drawing parallels to past antitrust cases against Microsoft and Google's own historical stance on default settings.

[sources/Apple_defends_Google_Search_deal_in_court_There_wasn_t_a_valid_alternative]
- The trial is titled US v. Google.
- Eddy Cue is a witness for Apple.
- Judge Amit Mehta presided over the case.
- The Information Services Agreement (ISA) has been in place since 2002.
- Cue negotiated the current ISA iteration in 2016.
- Google CEO Sundar Pichai was involved in the 2016 renegotiation.
- Meagan Bellshaw is a Justice Department lawyer.
- John Schmidtlein is a Google lawyer.
- Three iPhone screenshots were shown regarding setup process.
- Screenshots included the Appearance screen, location-tracking prompt, and App Tracking Transparency pop-up.
- DuckDuckGo's CEO testified previously claiming switching search engines takes too many steps.
- Safari was introduced in early 2003.
- Before 2003, users had to manually type google.com to search.
- Apple deals with Yahoo and Bing to make those services easy to find.
- The ISA represents a significant portion of Apple's profits.
- Specific revenue numbers were discussed in closed court sessions.
- Google pays Apple billions of dollars a year.
- Apple believes it has better privacy than Google.
- The ISA requires Google to allow searching without logging in.
- Apple makes it harder for Google to track users via Safari.
- The courtroom had a monitor malfunction during testimony.
- Judge Mehta joked about Apple making a donation if they wanted to switch.
- Cue stated Apple would never consider walking away from the deal if revenue share couldn't be agreed upon.
- Cue claimed he couldn't remember the names of some search engine alternatives.

Sam Bankman-Fried's criminal trial for seven counts of fraud and conspiracy against FTX has begun, following the exchange's collapse in November 2022 due to severe liquidity issues and mismanagement of customer funds. The once-valued $32 billion crypto empire filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy, leading to the arrest of Bankman-Fried and the guilty pleas of former executives Gary Wang and Caroline Ellison, while the trial proceeds with high-profile legal representation.

selected_passages.title: raw:sources/Is_Google_Search_better_than_the_rest_And_is_that_fair
selected_passages.text: For the US, which has to prove that Google somehow broke the law to achieve the status quo, this legal case could be an uphill battle. But for the rest of us, it offers a rare opportunity for some insight into what the tech giant does with its enormous market share. Is it still focused on being the best? Or, as has been alleged, does it use its ubiquity to squeeze us for money even at the expense of product quality? How ‘organic’ are Google’s results? This month, Wired posted an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray, which alleged that Google had accidentally revealed during the trial that it manipulates people’s search queries for maximum ad revenue. The example given was replacing a search for “children’s clothing” with “NIKOLAI-brand kidswear”. Loading Google rejected this in very strong terms, saying the piece was misleading and inaccurate while denying ever altering search terms. Wired removed the article for not meeting its standards, but the degree to which it was shared on social media and boosted in write-ups at other outlets shows just how willing people are to accept foul play on Google’s part. A suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling follows the company at all times.

For the US, which has to prove that Google somehow broke the law to achieve the status quo, this legal case could be an uphill battle. But for the rest of us, it offers a rare opportunity for some insight into what the tech giant does with its enormous market share. Is it still focused on being the best? Or, as has been alleged, does it use its ubiquity to squeeze us for money even at the expense of product quality? How ‘organic’ are Google’s results? This month, Wired posted an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray, which alleged that Google had accidentally revealed during the trial that it manipulates people’s search queries for maximum ad revenue. The example given was replacing a search for “children’s clothing” with “NIKOLAI-brand kidswear”. Loading Google rejected this in very strong terms, saying the piece was misleading and inaccurate while denying ever altering search terms. Wired removed the article for not meeting its standards, but the degree to which it was shared on social media and boosted in write-ups at other outlets shows just how willing people are to accept foul play on Google’s part. A suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling follows the company at all times.

- The case follows a recent agreement where Google pays Canadian media $73.5 million annually for content use.

- Yedidia has legal immunity during his testimony.
- Bankman-Fried spent about seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison.

A new class action lawsuit filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case, filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, argues that Google “siphons off” news publishers’ content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means. It also specifically cites new AI technologies like Google’s Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

selected_passages.title: sources/News_publisher_files_class_action_antitrust_suit_against_Google_citing_AI_s_harms_to_their_bottom_line
selected_passages.text: Helena World Chronicle, LLC has filed a class action antitrust lawsuit against Google and Alphabet in the U.S. District Court in D.C., alleging that Google's AI technologies, including Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard, along with older features like the Knowledge Graph, are siphoning content, readers, and ad revenue from news publishers. The suit claims these practices violate the Sherman Act and Clayton Act by discouraging users from visiting publisher websites, potentially causing publishers to lose 20-40% of their traffic, and seeks an injunction requiring consent for using publisher data to train AI models.

Helena World Chronicle, LLC has filed a class action antitrust lawsuit against Google and Alphabet in the U.S. District Court in D.C., alleging that Google's AI technologies, including Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard, along with older features like the Knowledge Graph, are siphoning content, readers, and ad revenue from news publishers. selected_passages.text: For the US, which has to prove that Google somehow broke the law to achieve the status quo, this legal case could be an uphill battle. But for the rest of us, it offers a rare opportunity for some insight into what the tech giant does with its enormous market share. Is it still focused on being the best? Or, as has been alleged, does it use its ubiquity to squeeze us for money even at the expense of product quality? How ‘organic’ are Google’s results? This month, Wired posted an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray, which alleged that Google had accidentally revealed during the trial that it manipulates people’s search queries for maximum ad revenue. The example given was replacing a search for “children’s clothing” with “NIKOLAI-brand kidswear”. Loading Google rejected this in very strong terms, saying the piece was misleading and inaccurate while denying ever altering search terms. Wired removed the article for not meeting its standards, but the degree to which it was shared on social media and boosted in write-ups at other outlets shows just how willing people are to accept foul play on Google’s part. A suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling follows the company at all times.

[raw:sources/Is_Google_Search_better_than_the_rest_And_is_that_fair]
For the US, which has to prove that Google somehow broke the law to achieve the status quo, this legal case could be an uphill battle. But for the rest of us, it offers a rare opportunity for some insight into what the tech giant does with its enormous market share. Is it still focused on being the best? Or, as has been alleged, does it use its ubiquity to squeeze us for money even at the expense of product quality? How ‘organic’ are Google’s results? This month, Wired posted an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray, which alleged that Google had accidentally revealed during the trial that it manipulates people’s search queries for maximum ad revenue. The example given was replacing a search for “children’s clothing” with “NIKOLAI-brand kidswear”. Loading Google rejected this in very strong terms, saying the piece was misleading and inaccurate while denying ever altering search terms. Wired removed the article for not meeting its standards, but the degree to which it was shared on social media and boosted in write-ups at other outlets shows just how willing people are to accept foul play on Google’s part. A suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling follows the company at all times.

Sam Bankman-Fried's criminal trial for seven counts of fraud and conspiracy against FTX has begun, following the exchange's collapse in November 2022 due to severe liquidity issues and mismanagement of customer funds. The once-valued $32 billion crypto empire filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy, leading to the arrest of Bankman-Fried and the guilty pleas of former executives Gary Wang and Caroline Ellison, while the trial proceeds with high-profile legal representation.

[sources/Is_Sam_Bankman-Fried_a_bad_man_or_a_good_boy_Lawyers_swap_opening_statements_before_first_witnesses_take_the_stand]

- Defense attorneys argued Bankman-Fried acted in good faith, built successful businesses, and did not defraud anyone.
- Witnesses included a victim who lost nearly $100,000 and a former friend who admitted to writing code that may have contributed to the scheme.
- The trial featured high-profile attendees including Bankman-Fried's parents, U.S. Attorney Damian Williams, and venture capitalist Matt Huang.
- Bankman-Fried spent seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison before this trial, resulting in more prominent cheekbones.

selected_passages.text:
- Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to make itself the default search engine.
- Approximately $18 billion of the payment went directly to Apple.
- Google's deal with Apple has been in place since 2003.
- When users switch their browser homepage to Google, they perform 15% more searches.
- When users switch away from Google, their searches drop by 27%.
- Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella offered to spend $15 billion annually to make Bing the default on Apple devices.
- Google gets 16 times more data than Bing every day.
- The DOJ accused Google of systematically destroying chat messages via the history-off option.
- Pichai changed the history-off default for chat in February to comply with a litigation hold.
- The trial is expected to continue for several weeks.
- The case is compared to the 1990s U.S. trial against Microsoft.
- If ruled against Google, the outcome could resemble the Microsoft settlement.
- Google might be required to turn over collected data to other search engines.
- The FTC sued Amazon in September for anticompetitive strategies.
- The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over its third-party app policies.
- There is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook regarding Instagram and WhatsApp.
- Google's legal chief David Drummond sent an angry letter to Microsoft in 2005.
- The letter accused Microsoft's Internet Explorer default setting as anticompetitive.
- Google's internal chat logs were deleted despite being subject to a litigation hold.
- Pichai testified on October 28 regarding the search head's revelations.
- The DOJ filed a separate claim in January alongside eight states.

selected_passages.text: A new class action lawsuit filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case, filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, argues that Google “siphons off” news publishers’ content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means. It also specifically cites new AI technologies like Google’s Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

A new class action lawsuit filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case, filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, argues that Google “siphons off” news publishers’ content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means. It also specifically cites new AI technologies like Google’s Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

selected_passages.title: sources/News_publisher_files_class_action_antitrust_suit_against_Google_citing_AI_s_harms_to_their_bottom_line
selected_passages.text: Helena World Chronicle, LLC has filed a class action antitrust lawsuit against Google and Alphabet in the U.S. District Court in D.C., alleging that Google's AI technologies, including Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard, along with older features like the Knowledge Graph, are siphoning content, readers, and ad revenue from news publishers. The suit claims these practices violate the Sherman Act and Clayton Act by discouraging users from visiting publisher websites, potentially causing publishers to lose 20-40% of their traffic, and seeks an injunction requiring consent for using publisher data to train AI models.

FTX co-founder and former CTO Gary Wang, and Alameda Research’s former CEO, Caroline Ellison, both pleaded guilty in December 2022 to federal criminal charges in relation to the FTX collapse. They’re also facing civil penalties from the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) alongside the criminal charges. Wang and Ellison plan to cooperate with prosecutors and will be major witnesses in the trial, given their close ties to Bankman-Fried, FTX and Alameda.

Sam Bankman-Fried's criminal trial for seven counts of fraud and conspiracy against FTX has begun, following the exchange's collapse in November 2022 due to severe liquidity issues and mismanagement of customer funds. selected_passages.text: Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified in a U.S. antitrust trial defending the company's $26.3 billion spending to secure default search engine status across platforms, including a major deal with Apple. The Department of Justice argues these tactics block competition and hinder rivals from accessing necessary data, drawing parallels to past antitrust cases against Microsoft and Google's own historical stance on default settings.

Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified in a U.S. antitrust trial defending the company's $26.3 billion spending to secure default search engine status across platforms, including a major deal with Apple. The Department of Justice argues these tactics block competition and hinder rivals from accessing necessary data, drawing parallels to past antitrust cases against Microsoft and Google's own historical stance on default settings.

selected_passages.title: sources/5_things_we_learned_so_far_about_the_Google_antitrust_case
selected_passages.text:
- Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to make itself the default search engine.
- Approximately $18 billion of the payment went directly to Apple.
- Google's deal with Apple has been in place since 2003.
- When users switch their browser homepage to Google, they perform 15% more searches.
- When users switch away from Google, their searches drop by 27%.
- Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella offered to spend $15 billion annually to make Bing the default on Apple devices.
- Google gets 16 times more data than Bing every day.
- The DOJ accused Google of systematically destroying chat messages via the history-off option.
- Pichai changed the history-off default for chat in February to comply with a litigation hold.
- The trial is expected to continue for several weeks.
- The case is compared to the 1990s U.S. trial against Microsoft.
- If ruled against Google, the outcome could resemble the Microsoft settlement.
- Google might be required to turn over collected data to other search engines.
- The FTC sued Amazon in September for anticompetitive strategies.
- The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over its third-party app policies.
- There is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook regarding Instagram and WhatsApp.
- Google's legal chief David Drummond sent an angry letter to Microsoft in 2005.
- The letter accused Microsoft's Internet Explorer default setting as anticompetitive.
- Google's internal chat logs were deleted despite being subject to a litigation hold.
- Pichai testified on October 28 regarding the search head's revelations.
- The DOJ filed a separate claim in January alongside eight states.

context:
[sources/5_things_we_learned_so_far_about_the_Google_antitrust_case]
Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified in a U.S. antitrust trial defending the company's $26.3 billion spending to secure default search engine status across platforms, including a major deal with Apple. The Department of Justice argues these tactics block competition and hinder rivals from accessing necessary data, drawing parallels to past antitrust cases against Microsoft and Google's own historical stance on default settings.

[sources/5_things_we_learned_so_far_about_the_Google_antitrust_case]
- Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to make itself the default search engine.
- Approximately $18 billion of the payment went directly to Apple.
- Google's deal with Apple has been in place since 2003.
- When users switch their browser homepage to Google, they perform 15% more searches.
- When users switch away from Google, their searches drop by 27%.
- Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella offered to spend $15 billion annually to make Bing the default on Apple devices.
- Google gets 16 times more data than Bing every day.
- The DOJ accused Google of systematically destroying chat messages via the history-off option.
- Pichai changed the history-off default for chat in February to comply with a litigation hold.
- The trial is expected to continue for several weeks.
- The case is compared to the 1990s U.S. trial against Microsoft.
- If ruled against Google, the outcome could resemble the Microsoft settlement.
- Google might be required to turn over collected data to other search engines.
- The FTC sued Amazon in September for anticompetitive strategies.
- The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over its third-party app policies.
- There is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook regarding Instagram and WhatsApp.
- Google's legal chief David Drummond sent an angry letter to Microsoft in 2005.
- The letter accused Microsoft's Internet Explorer default setting as anticompetitive.
- Google's internal chat logs were deleted despite being subject to a litigation hold.
- Pichai testified on October 28 regarding the search head's revelations.
- The DOJ filed a separate claim in January alongside eight states.

[raw:sources/Apple_defends_Google_Search_deal_in_court_There_wasn_t_a_valid_alternative]
Cue was on the stand as a witness in US v. Google, the landmark antitrust trial over Google’s search business. Cue is one of the highest-profile witnesses in the case so far, in part because the deal between Google and Apple — which makes Google the default search engine on all Apple devices and pays Apple billions of dollars a year — is central to the US Department of Justice’s case against Google.

[sources/Apple_defends_Google_Search_deal_in_court_There_wasn_t_a_valid_alternative]
- Eddy Cue testified that there was no valid alternative to Google Search for Apple devices at the time of the deal.
- The Information Services Agreement (ISA) makes Google the default search engine on Apple products in exchange for billions in payments.
- Apple believes in protecting user privacy but also maintains a strong partnership with Google, creating a central tension in the trial.
- Cue argued that showing users alternative search engines during setup would degrade the user experience and slow down device onboarding.
- The Justice Department questions whether Apple's choice of Google is based on product quality or financial incentives.

[sources/5_things_we_learned_so_far_about_the_Google_antitrust_case]
- Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 to become the default search engine on various platforms.
- The Department of Justice claims Google's dominance hinders competitors by blocking access to advertising and search data.
- Google agreed not to promote Chrome to Safari users as part of its deal with Apple.
- Pichai admitted attempting to get Google preinstalled on iPhones in 2018, which Apple declined.
- The trial highlights Google's hypocrisy regarding default search engine settings compared to its past actions against Microsoft.

The case, filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, argues that Google “siphons off” news publishers’ content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means. selected_passages.title: raw:sources/Is_Google_Search_better_than_the_rest_And_is_that_fair
selected_passages.text: For the US, which has to prove that Google somehow broke the law to achieve the status quo, this legal case could be an uphill battle. But for the rest of us, it offers a rare opportunity for some insight into what the tech giant does with its enormous market share. Is it still focused on being the best? Or, as has been alleged, does it use its ubiquity to squeeze us for money even at the expense of product quality? How ‘organic’ are Google’s results? This month, Wired posted an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray, which alleged that Google had accidentally revealed during the trial that it manipulates people’s search queries for maximum ad revenue. The example given was replacing a search for “children’s clothing” with “NIKOLAI-brand kidswear”. Loading Google rejected this in very strong terms, saying the piece was misleading and inaccurate while denying ever altering search terms. Wired removed the article for not meeting its standards, but the degree to which it was shared on social media and boosted in write-ups at other outlets shows just how willing people are to accept foul play on Google’s part. A suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling follows the company at all times.

[raw:sources/News_publisher_files_class_action_antitrust_suit_against_Google_citing_AI_s_harms_to_their_bottom_line]
A new class action lawsuit filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case, filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, argues that Google “siphons off” news publishers’ content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means. It also specifically cites new AI technologies like Google’s Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

[sources/News_publisher_files_class_action_antitrust_suit_against_Google_citing_AI_s_harms_to_their_bottom_line]
Helena World Chronicle, LLC has filed a class action antitrust lawsuit against Google and Alphabet in the U.S. District Court in D.C., alleging that Google's AI technologies, including Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard, along with older features like the Knowledge Graph, are siphoning content, readers, and ad revenue from news publishers. The suit claims these practices violate the Sherman Act and Clayton Act by discouraging users from visiting publisher websites, potentially causing publishers to lose 20-40% of their traffic, and seeks an injunction requiring consent for using publisher data to train AI models.

[sources/News_publisher_files_class_action_antitrust_suit_against_Google_citing_AI_s_harms_to_their_bottom_line]

- Reports suggest publishers could lose 20-40% of website traffic when Google's AI products fully roll out.
- The case follows a recent agreement where Google pays Canadian media $73.5 million annually for content use.

[raw:sources/Is_Google_Search_better_than_the_rest_And_is_that_fair]
For the US, which has to prove that Google somehow broke the law to achieve the status quo, this legal case could be an uphill battle. But for the rest of us, it offers a rare opportunity for some insight into what the tech giant does with its enormous market share. Is it still focused on being the best? Or, as has been alleged, does it use its ubiquity to squeeze us for money even at the expense of product quality? How ‘organic’ are Google’s results? This month, Wired posted an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray, which alleged that Google had accidentally revealed during the trial that it manipulates people’s search queries for maximum ad revenue. The example given was replacing a search for “children’s clothing” with “NIKOLAI-brand kidswear”. Loading Google rejected this in very strong terms, saying the piece was misleading and inaccurate while denying ever altering search terms. Wired removed the article for not meeting its standards, but the degree to which it was shared on social media and boosted in write-ups at other outlets shows just how willing people are to accept foul play on Google’s part. A suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling follows the company at all times.

selected_passages.title: raw:sources/Is_Google_Search_better_than_the_rest_And_is_that_fair
selected_passages.text: For the US, which has to prove that Google somehow broke the law to achieve the status quo, this legal case could be an uphill battle. But for the rest of us, it offers a rare opportunity for some insight into what the tech giant does with its enormous market share. Is it still focused on being the best? Or, as has been alleged, does it use its ubiquity to squeeze us for money even at the expense of product quality? How ‘organic’ are Google’s results? This month, Wired posted an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray, which alleged that Google had accidentally revealed during the trial that it manipulates people’s search queries for maximum ad revenue. The example given was replacing a search for “children’s clothing” with “NIKOLAI-brand kidswear”. Loading Google rejected this in very strong terms, saying the piece was misleading and inaccurate while denying ever altering search terms. Wired removed the article for not meeting its standards, but the degree to which it was shared on social media and boosted in write-ups at other outlets shows just how willing people are to accept foul play on Google’s part. A suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling follows the company at all times.

selected_passages.title: raw:sources/Is_Google_Search_better_than_the_rest_And_is_that_fair
selected_passages.text: Grey herself is a former vice-president at DuckDuckGo, a privacy-focused company founded explicitly to counter giants such as Google. She admits that she may have misinterpreted the evidence, but maintains that Google manipulates Search to maximise ad revenue. So what does Google say? In a post on X, Google’s official search liaison, Danny Sullivan, said ad systems do not affect the organic results, i.e. the list of blue links in search results that are not sponsored. “Ad keyword matching is a long-standing and well-known process that is designed to connect people to relevant ads. A separate process, which has nothing to do with ads, is used to match organic results to a query,” he said. “It’s no secret that Google Search looks beyond the specific words in a query to better understand their meaning ... If you make a spelling mistake, or search for a term that’s not on a page but where the page has a close synonym, or if you aren’t even sure exactly how to search for something, our meaning matching systems help.” It is true that some search queries result in more ads than others, and what ads you get can vary wildly depending on your request, which is the result of the keyword matching Google uses to sell ads. But Google denies pushing users towards the most monetisable subjects.

Helena World Chronicle, LLC has filed a class action antitrust lawsuit against Google and Alphabet in the U.S. District Court in D.C., alleging that Google's AI technologies, including Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard, along with older features like the Knowledge Graph, are siphoning content, readers, and ad revenue from news publishers. The suit claims these practices violate the Sherman Act and Clayton Act by discouraging users from visiting publisher websites, potentially causing publishers to lose 20-40% of their traffic, and seeks an injunction requiring consent for using publisher data to train AI models.

[raw:sources/News_publisher_files_class_action_antitrust_suit_against_Google_citing_AI_s_harms_to_their_bottom_line]
A new class action lawsuit filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case, filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, argues that Google “siphons off” news publishers’ content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means. It also specifically cites new AI technologies like Google’s Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

[sources/News_publisher_files_class_action_antitrust_suit_against_Google_citing_AI_s_harms_to_their_bottom_line]
- Helena World Chronicle filed a class action antitrust suit against Google and Alphabet in the U.S. District Court in D.C.
- The lawsuit alleges Google uses AI technologies like SGE and Bard to misappropriate publisher content and reduce traffic to news sites.
- Plaintiffs claim Google's actions violate the Sherman Act and Clayton Act, seeking monetary and injunctive relief.
- Reports suggest publishers could lose 20-40% of website traffic when Google's AI products fully roll out.
- The case follows a recent agreement where Google pays Canadian media $73.5 million annually for content use.

[raw:sources/Is_Google_Search_better_than_the_rest_And_is_that_fair]
For the US, which has to prove that Google somehow broke the law to achieve the status quo, this legal case could be an uphill battle. But for the rest of us, it offers a rare opportunity for some insight into what the tech giant does with its enormous market share. Is it still focused on being the best? Or, as has been alleged, does it use its ubiquity to squeeze us for money even at the expense of product quality? How ‘organic’ are Google’s results? This month, Wired posted an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray, which alleged that Google had accidentally revealed during the trial that it manipulates people’s search queries for maximum ad revenue. The example given was replacing a search for “children’s clothing” with “NIKOLAI-brand kidswear”. Loading Google rejected this in very strong terms, saying the piece was misleading and inaccurate while denying ever altering search terms. Wired removed the article for not meeting its standards, but the degree to which it was shared on social media and boosted in write-ups at other outlets shows just how willing people are to accept foul play on Google’s part. A suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling follows the company at all times.

- Google's extensive data collection on searches and interactions is a primary advantage for personalization but a point of contention for privacy advocates.
- Legal challenges to Google's default status face hurdles because users often actively choose Google over other providers despite initial defaults.
- Allegations exist that Google manipulates search queries to maximize ad revenue, though Google denies altering organic results.
- The volume of indexed data has grown exponentially from 9 ZB in 2013 to over 120 ZB in 2023, changing the nature of search results.
- Google utilizes machine learning and semantic matching to refine queries, while critics argue this widens the content pool to favor monetization.

- The Justice Department questions whether Apple's choice of Google is based on product quality or financial incentives.

selected_passages.title: sources/5_things_we_learned_so_far_about_the_Google_antitrust_case
selected_passages.text:
- Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to make itself the default search engine.
- Approximately $18 billion of the payment went directly to Apple.
- Google's deal with Apple has been in place since 2003.
- When users switch their browser homepage to Google, they perform 15% more searches.
- When users switch away from Google, their searches drop by 27%.
- Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella offered to spend $15 billion annually to make Bing the default on Apple devices.
- Google gets 16 times more data than Bing every day.
- The DOJ accused Google of systematically destroying chat messages via the history-off option.
- Pichai changed the history-off default for chat in February to comply with a litigation hold.
- The trial is expected to continue for several weeks.
- The case is compared to the 1990s U.S. trial against Microsoft.
- If ruled against Google, the outcome could resemble the Microsoft settlement.
- Google might be required to turn over collected data to other search engines.
- The FTC sued Amazon in September for anticompetitive strategies.
- The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over its third-party app policies.
- There is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook regarding Instagram and WhatsApp.
- Google's legal chief David Drummond sent an angry letter to Microsoft in 2005.
- The letter accused Microsoft's Internet Explorer default setting as anticompetitive.
- Google's internal chat logs were deleted despite being subject to a litigation hold.
- Pichai testified on October 28 regarding the search head's revelations.
- The DOJ filed a separate claim in January alongside eight states.

[raw:sources/News_publisher_files_class_action_antitrust_suit_against_Google_citing_AI_s_harms_to_their_bottom_line]
A new class action lawsuit filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case, filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, argues that Google “siphons off” news publishers’ content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means. It also specifically cites new AI technologies like Google’s Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

[sources/5_things_we_learned_so_far_about_the_Google_antitrust_case]
- Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to make itself the default search engine.
- Approximately $18 billion of the payment went directly to Apple.
- Google's deal with Apple has been in place since 2003.
- When users switch their browser homepage to Google, they perform 15% more searches.
- When users switch away from Google, their searches drop by 27%.
- Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella offered to spend $15 billion annually to make Bing the default on Apple devices.
- Google gets 16 times more data than Bing every day.
- The DOJ accused Google of systematically destroying chat messages via the history-off option.
- Pichai changed the history-off default for chat in February to comply with a litigation hold.
- The trial is expected to continue for several weeks.
- The case is compared to the 1990s U.S. trial against Microsoft.
- If ruled against Google, the outcome could resemble the Microsoft settlement.
- Google might be required to turn over collected data to other search engines.
- The FTC sued Amazon in September for anticompetitive strategies.
- The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over its third-party app policies.
- There is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook regarding Instagram and WhatsApp.
- Google's legal chief David Drummond sent an angry letter to Microsoft in 2005.
- The letter accused Microsoft's Internet Explorer default setting as anticompetitive.
- Google's internal chat logs were deleted despite being subject to a litigation hold.
- Pichai testified on October 28 regarding the search head's revelations.
- The DOJ filed a separate claim in January alongside eight states.

A new class action lawsuit filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case, filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, argues that Google “siphons off” news publishers’ content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means. It also specifically cites new AI technologies like Google’s Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

selected_passages.title: sources/News_publisher_files_class_action_antitrust_suit_against_Google_citing_AI_s_harms_to_their_bottom_line
selected_passages.text: Helena World Chronicle, LLC has filed a class action antitrust lawsuit against Google and Alphabet in the U.S. District Court in D.C., alleging that Google's AI technologies, including Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard, along with older features like the Knowledge Graph, are siphoning content, readers, and ad revenue from news publishers. The suit claims these practices violate the Sherman Act and Clayton Act by discouraging users from visiting publisher websites, potentially causing publishers to lose 20-40% of their traffic, and seeks an injunction requiring consent for using publisher data to train AI models.

Helena World Chronicle, LLC has filed a class action antitrust lawsuit against Google and Alphabet in the U.S. District Court in D.C., alleging that Google's AI technologies, including Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard, along with older features like the Knowledge Graph, are siphoning content, readers, and ad revenue from news publishers. The suit claims these practices violate the Sherman Act and Clayton Act by discouraging users from visiting publisher websites, potentially causing publishers to lose 20-40% of their traffic, and seeks an injunction requiring consent for using publisher data to train AI models.

selected_passages.text: Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified in a U.S. antitrust trial defending the company's $26.3 billion spending to secure default search engine status across platforms, including a major deal with Apple. selected_passages.context_block:

Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified in a U.S. antitrust trial defending the company's $26.3 billion spending to secure default search engine status across platforms, including a major deal with Apple. The Department of Justice argues these tactics block competition and hinder rivals from accessing necessary data, drawing parallels to past antitrust cases against Microsoft and Google's own historical stance on default settings.

selected_passages.title: sources/5_things_we_learned_so_far_about_the_Google_antitrust_case
selected_passages.text:
- Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to make itself the default search engine.
- Approximately $18 billion of the payment went directly to Apple.
- Google's deal with Apple has been in place since 2003.
- When users switch their browser homepage to Google, they perform 15% more searches.
- When users switch away from Google, their searches drop by 27%.
- Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella offered to spend $15 billion annually to make Bing the default on Apple devices.
- Google gets 16 times more data than Bing every day.
- The DOJ accused Google of systematically destroying chat messages via the history-off option.
- Pichai changed the history-off default for chat in February to comply with a litigation hold.
- The trial is expected to continue for several weeks.
- The case is compared to the 1990s U.S. trial against Microsoft.
- If ruled against Google, the outcome could resemble the Microsoft settlement.
- Google might be required to turn over collected data to other search engines.
- The FTC sued Amazon in September for anticompetitive strategies.
- The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over its third-party app policies.
- There is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook regarding Instagram and WhatsApp.
- Google's legal chief David Drummond sent an angry letter to Microsoft in 2005.
- The letter accused Microsoft's Internet Explorer default setting as anticompetitive.
- Google's internal chat logs were deleted despite being subject to a litigation hold.
- Pichai testified on October 28 regarding the search head's revelations.
- The DOJ filed a separate claim in January alongside eight states.

A new class action lawsuit filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case, filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, argues that Google “siphons off” news publishers’ content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means. It also specifically cites new AI technologies like Google’s Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

[sources/News_publisher_files_class_action_antitrust_suit_against_Google_citing_AI_s_harms_to_their_bottom_line]
Helena World Chronicle, LLC has filed a class action antitrust lawsuit against Google and Alphabet in the U.S. District Court in D.C., alleging that Google's AI technologies, including Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard, along with older features like the Knowledge Graph, are siphoning content, readers, and ad revenue from news publishers. The suit claims these practices violate the Sherman Act and Clayton Act by discouraging users from visiting publisher websites, potentially causing publishers to lose 20-40% of their traffic, and seeks an injunction requiring consent for using publisher data to train AI models.

[sources/5_things_we_learned_so_far_about_the_Google_antitrust_case]
Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified in a U.S. antitrust trial defending the company's $26.3 billion spending to secure default search engine status across platforms, including a major deal with Apple. The Department of Justice argues these tactics block competition and hinder rivals from accessing necessary data, drawing parallels to past antitrust cases against Microsoft and Google's own historical stance on default settings.

[sources/5_things_we_learned_so_far_about_the_Google_antitrust_case]
- Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to make itself the default search engine.
- Approximately $18 billion of the payment went directly to Apple.
- Google's deal with Apple has been in place since 2003.
- When users switch their browser homepage to Google, they perform 15% more searches.
- When users switch away from Google, their searches drop by 27%.
- Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella offered to spend $15 billion annually to make Bing the default on Apple devices.
- Google gets 16 times more data than Bing every day.
- The DOJ accused Google of systematically destroying chat messages via the history-off option.
- Pichai changed the history-off default for chat in February to comply with a litigation hold.
- The trial is expected to continue for several weeks.
- The case is compared to the 1990s U.S. trial against Microsoft.
- If ruled against Google, the outcome could resemble the Microsoft settlement.
- Google might be required to turn over collected data to other search engines.
- The FTC sued Amazon in September for anticompetitive strategies.
- The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over its third-party app policies.
- There is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook regarding Instagram and WhatsApp.
- Google's legal chief David Drummond sent an angry letter to Microsoft in 2005.
- The letter accused Microsoft's Internet Explorer default setting as anticompetitive.
- Google's internal chat logs were deleted despite being subject to a litigation hold.
- Pichai testified on October 28 regarding the search head's revelations.
- The DOJ filed a separate claim in January alongside eight states.

selected_passages.text: A new class action lawsuit filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case, filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, argues that Google “siphons off” news publishers’ content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means. It also specifically cites new AI technologies like Google’s Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.
